1.1.listen: Trace the melody with your hand while it plays: up when it climbs, down when it falls. That's pitch.
1.1.guitar: Play the low E string open, then the high E string open. Same letter, two octaves apart in pitch.

songs.title: Golden
songs.artist: HUNTR/X, EJAE, AUDREY NUNA, REI AMI & KPop Demon Hunters Cast

1.2.listen: Hum the first note of the chorus, then find it on your guitar and name its letter, A to G.
1.2.guitar: Play the open strings from low to high and say each letter out loud: E A D G B E.

1.3.listen: Sing the hook, then sing it again higher or lower until it's comfortable. Same notes in a different octave.
1.3.guitar: Play A on the open A string, then A at fret 2 of the G string. They're an octave apart.

1.4.listen: While it plays, try F and then F♯ on your guitar. One of them clashes and one fits. A sharp is one fret higher.
1.4.guitar: On the high E string, F is fret 1 and F♯ is fret 2. One fret is one half step.

1.5.listen: Find the song's home note on your guitar. If that fret is a sharp or flat, give it both of its names.
1.5.guitar: Fret 4 on the A string is C♯, and it's also D♭. One fret, two names.

songs.title: On The Ground
songs.note: In D♭ major. D♭ is also called C♯.

2.1.listen: Slide one finger up a string one fret at a time while it plays. Each fret is a half step. Stop when a note fits the song.
2.1.guitar: On the B string, fret 1 to fret 2 is a half step, and fret 1 to fret 3 is a whole step.

2.2.listen: Find the home note, then sing do-re-mi up from it. If the scale fits the song, the song is in a major key.
2.2.guitar: Play the C major scale in open position: C (A string, fret 3), D, E, F, G, A, B, C.

songs.title: we can't be friends (wait for your love)

2.3.listen: Each of these is in a major key. Count the flats in its key signature.
2.3.guitar: Put a capo on fret 1 and play the open C major scale. Now you're playing D♭ major, with five flats.

songs.title: On The Ground
songs.note: D♭ major: 5 flats (B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭).

3.1.listen: Play a minor song and a major song back to back. The minor one has a lowered 3rd, so home sounds darker.
3.1.guitar: Strum Am, then A. The only change is one note: the 3rd, C or C♯.

songs.title: REBEL HEART
songs.note: Your ear test: does the chorus feel darker like good 4 u, or brighter like drivers license?

3.2.listen: Relative keys share a key signature. Every major key has a minor key that starts on its 6th note.
3.2.guitar: Put a capo on fret 4 and strum Bm, A, D, G. Those shapes sound as Lovesick Girls' D♯m, C♯, F♯, B.

songs.title: Lovesick Girls
songs.note: D♯ minor and F♯ major share 6 sharps. The chorus pulls between the two.

songs.title: Bad Liar
songs.note: Hum the note the song keeps coming home to. Then try the note 3 half steps above it: if that fits, you're hearing the relative major.

songs.title: Yeah Yeah Yeah
songs.note: Listen for the home chord. Does it sound minor (dark) or major (bright)?

3.3.listen: Hum the home note (the tonic), then the note five steps above it (the dominant). Hear how the dominant wants to go home?
3.3.guitar: In A minor: play A (open A string), then E (open low E string or fret 2 on the D string). Tonic, then dominant.

4.1.listen: Count 1, 2, 3, 4 along with the beat. Where does your count start over? That's the start of a bar.
4.1.guitar: Strum Em down on every beat, 4 strums per bar, and count out loud.

4.2.listen: Clap along with the kick drum, then try clapping twice as fast. You've gone from quarter notes to eighth notes.
4.2.guitar: Hold Em for 4 beats (a whole note), then strum it 2, 4 and 8 times in the same space.

4.3.listen: Find a note the singer holds in the chorus. Count how many beats it lasts. Longer than one value? That's a dot or a tie.
4.3.guitar: Strum G, let it ring for 1½ beats (a dotted quarter), then strum again on the 'and' of 2.

4.4.listen: Tap the beat. Does it feel like 1-2, 1-2 or like 1-2-3, 1-2-3? That's the meter.
4.4.guitar: Strum C as a waltz (1-2-3), then in 4 (1-2-3-4). Feel how different they are.

4.5.listen: Try fitting three even claps into one beat of the song. That's a triplet: three in the space of two.
4.5.guitar: Mute the strings with your fretting hand and strum three even strokes per beat: tri-pl-et, tri-pl-et.

4.6.listen: Write the rhythm of the hook's first bar so each beat is easy to see. Group the notes beat by beat.
4.6.guitar: Play the hook's rhythm on one muted string while counting the beats out loud.

5.1.listen: Sing the first two notes of the chorus. Count the letter names from one to the other, both included. That's the interval's size.
5.1.guitar: On the A string, fret 0 to fret 2 is a 2nd (A to B), and fret 0 to fret 4 is a 3rd (A to C♯).

5.2.listen: Hum the home note, then the highest note of the hook. Count up the major scale from home to name the interval.
5.2.guitar: A perfect 5th: the open A string, then fret 2 on the D string (E).

5.3.listen: Pick a note from the hook and build a major 3rd above it on your guitar. Does it fit the song?
5.3.guitar: Major 3rd: fret 3 on the A string (C), then fret 2 on the D string (E).

5.4.listen: Sing a leap up from the hook, then sing it with the top note dropped an octave. The interval flips: a 3rd becomes a 6th.
5.4.guitar: C up to E is a 3rd (A string fret 3, D string fret 2). E up to C is a 6th (D string fret 2, B string fret 1). 3 + 6 = 9.

songs.title: hate that i made you love me

5.5.listen: Listen for a tense, edgy spot in the song. Augmented and diminished intervals, like the tritone, often make that sound.
5.5.guitar: A tritone: the open A string with fret 1 on the D string (D♯). Then resolve to E (D string, fret 2).

6.1.listen: Find one chord that fits the chorus, then name its root, 3rd and 5th.
6.1.guitar: Strum C, then play its notes one at a time: C (A string, fret 3), E (D string, fret 2), G (open G).

6.2.listen: Look up the song's chords and read each symbol: a plain letter is major, m is minor, ° is diminished, + is augmented.
6.2.guitar: Strum C, then Cm (barre at fret 3, Am shape). Hear the 3rd drop a half step.

6.3.listen: Listen to the bass. Does it always play the chord's root, or does it sometimes sit on the 3rd or 5th? That's an inversion.
6.3.guitar: Play C/E: the open C shape, but strum from the open low E string so E is in the bass.

6.4.listen: Pick one chord from the song and name three things: its root, its quality and its bass note.
6.4.guitar: Strum Am and name it: root A, minor, A in the bass. Then play it from the low E string: Am/E.

6.5.listen: Listen for a chord that sounds open and unsettled before it lands. Swapping the 3rd for a 4th or 2nd makes that sus sound.
6.5.guitar: Strum D, then Dsus4 (fret 3 on the high E string), then back to D.

7.1.listen: Count the chords in the chorus loop and give each a number, starting from home as I.
7.1.guitar: In C, play I–IV–V–I: C, F, G, C. Say the numbers out loud as you strum.

7.2.listen: Find the home chord of the chorus, then count up the scale to name the other chords: I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi.
7.2.guitar: Play all seven chords of C major in order: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, Bdim (x2343x).

7.3.listen: Does the chorus sit on a minor home chord? Listen for whether the chord before home sounds major (V) or minor (v).
7.3.guitar: Play A minor's chords: Am, Bdim, C, Dm, Em, F, G. Then swap Em for E and hear the stronger pull back to Am.

7.4.listen: At the end of each phrase, ask: does it sound finished, or left hanging? Finished is usually V to I.
7.4.guitar: Play G then C (an authentic cadence), then C then G (a half cadence). Hear which one feels done.

8.1.listen: Listen for chords that sound softer or jazzier than plain triads. That extra color is often a seventh.
8.1.guitar: Compare C (x32010) with Cmaj7 (x32000), then G (320003) with G7 (320001).

8.2.listen: Listen for a chord that floats before it settles. That soft, open pull is the IV/5 sus sound.
8.2.guitar: Play F/G, an F chord over a low G (3x3211), then resolve it to C.

8.3.listen: Pick one chord in the verse and decide: major 7th, minor 7th, or dominant 7th?
8.3.guitar: Play C major's sevenths: Cmaj7 (x32000), Dm7 (xx0211), Em7 (022030), Fmaj7 (xx3210), G7 (320001), Am7 (x02010).

9.1.listen: Follow the bass in the chorus. Does it keep falling by fifths (or rising by fourths) toward home?
9.1.guitar: Play Am, Dm, G, C. Each root falls a fifth on the way home.

9.2.listen: Tap each time the chord changes. Is it every bar, or every two beats? Compare the verse with the chorus.
9.2.guitar: Strum C for 4 beats then G for 4. Then switch every 2 beats and feel the energy rise.

9.3.listen: Listen for a short trip home: a chord that leads to the dominant, then the dominant, then home.
9.3.guitar: Play ii–V–I in C: Dm, G, C. Then try it in G: Am, D, G.

9.4.listen: Sort the chorus chords into home (tonic), going away (pre-dominant) and pulling back (dominant).
9.4.guitar: Play C (home), F (away), G (pull), C (home), and name each job as you go.

9.5.listen: Listen for a short idea that repeats a step lower or higher each time. That's a sequence.
9.5.guitar: Play Am, Dm, G, C, F, Bdim (x2343x), E, Am: the same pattern stepping down.

9.6.listen: Listen for a big major chord a whole step below home. That's the ♭VII rock sound.
9.6.guitar: In G major, play G, F, C, G. The F is ♭VII.

9.7.listen: Try singing the chorus over I–V–vi–IV. Does it fit, or does the song change the order?
9.7.guitar: Play C, G, Am, F on loop. Then try it in G: G, D, Em, C.

9.8.listen: Listen for a minor home chord that steps down and back up: i, VII, VI, VII.
9.8.guitar: Play Am, G, F, G on loop. Then try Em, D, C, D.

10.1.listen: Pick a long held note in the melody and ask: is it in the chord underneath? If not, it's a non-chord tone.
10.1.guitar: Hold a C chord and hum D over it. Hear the clash, then slide to C or E so it fits.

10.2.listen: Listen for the melody walking step by step between two chord notes. The note in the middle is a passing tone.
10.2.guitar: Over C, play C (A string, fret 3), D (open D), E (D string, fret 2). D is the passing tone.

10.3.listen: Listen for a note that steps away and comes right back. That's a neighbor tone.
10.3.guitar: Over G, play G (open G), A (G string, fret 2), G. A is the upper neighbor.

10.4.listen: Listen for a note that leaps onto a clash, then steps down into the chord. That's an appoggiatura.
10.4.guitar: Over C, play G (open G), leap to F (high E, fret 1), then step down to E (open high E).

10.5.listen: Listen for a note that steps away from a chord note, then leaps off the other way. That's an escape tone.
10.5.guitar: Over G, play B (open B), step to C (B string, fret 1), then leap down to G (open G).

10.6.listen: Listen for a note circled from above and below before it comes back. That's a double neighbor.
10.6.guitar: Over C, play C (B string, fret 1), D (B string, fret 3), B (open B), C (B string, fret 1).

10.7.listen: Listen for a melody note that shows up just before its chord does. That's an anticipation.
10.7.guitar: Strum C for a bar. On the last half-beat, play a G note early, then strum G.

10.8.listen: Listen for one low note that stays put while the chords change above it. That's a pedal point.
10.8.guitar: Let the open low E ring while you play E (022100), A/E (002220), and back to E.

10.9.listen: Listen for a held note that clashes with the new chord, then slips down into it. That's a suspension.
10.9.guitar: Play Dsus4 (xx0233), then D (xx0232). The G resolves down to F♯.

11.1.listen: Find the shortest catchy bit of the hook that keeps coming back. That's the motive.
11.1.guitar: Play the motive C–D–E (A string fret 3, open D, D string fret 2) twice.

11.2.listen: Listen for the hook coming back a little different: higher, lower, or with a new rhythm.
11.2.guitar: Play C–D–E, then move it up a step: D–E–F♯ (open D, D string frets 2 and 4).

11.3.listen: Listen for just the first two or three notes of the hook, repeated on their own. That's a fragment.
11.3.guitar: Play C–D–E–G, then only the fragment C–D, C–D.

11.4.listen: Count how many bars the first line lasts before the singer breathes. That's one phrase.
11.4.guitar: Strum C, F, G, C, one bar each: a 4-bar phrase that ends at home.

songs.title: you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love

11.5.listen: Split the first line into two halves. Where's the small pause in the middle?
11.5.guitar: Strum C, F (2 bars), pause, then G, C (2 bars). Each half is a subphrase.

12.1.listen: Map the song: mark where each verse, pre-chorus and chorus starts.
12.1.guitar: Play Am, F for a verse, then C, G for a chorus, and feel the lift.

12.2.listen: Listen for one section twice, a contrasting one, then the first again: A A B A.
12.2.guitar: Play C, Am, F, G twice (A A), then F, G (B), then C, Am, F, G (A).

12.3.listen: Does the second half start like the first, then go somewhere new? That's A B A C.
12.3.guitar: Play C, G (A), F, G (B), C, G (A), F, C (C).

12.4.listen: Count bars in the verse. Does the chord change to IV at bar 5, like a blues?
12.4.guitar: Play a 12-bar blues in A: A for 4 bars, D for 2, A for 2, then E, D, A, E.

12.5.listen: At the end of each section, does it land home (closed) or leave you hanging (open)?
12.5.guitar: End a phrase on C (closed), then end one on G (open), and hear the difference.
